newsitem.title: UK: British soldier killed in suspected IRA attack.
newsitem.headline: British soldier killed in suspected IRA attack.

text.p: A British soldier was shot dead in a suspected IRA guerrilla attack on Wednesday night, the first 1997 casualty of their campaign to end British rule of Northern Ireland.

Police said a civilian was also injured in the attack which took place at Bessbrook, site of a major British army base and a helicopter port for security forces patrolling the border area with the Irish republic.
The soldier who died was manning a checkpoint at the entry to the village, police said. He was killed by a single bullet. Further details were not immediately available.
Armagh is known by security forces as "bandit country" because of frequent IRA attacks. An IRA sniper or snipers was very active in the area in 1993 and 1994, police recalled.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, which bore the hallmarks of the Irish Republican Army, which seeks to unite the province with Ireland.
It was the first fatality in Northern Ireland since the IRA bombed Britain's army headquarters at Lisburn, near Belfast, in October last year, killing a soldier and injuring 30.
The Bessbrook shooting took place three days after the first anniversary of a London IRA bomb which ended the guerrillas' 17- month cease-fire.
It raised immediate fears of revenge attacks by Protestant Loyalist gunmen battling to maintain British rule.
Loyalists, the IRA's arch-foes, have abided by their own 1994 cease-fire but have said in media interviews that they will go back on the warpath if the IRA kills anyone.
All IRA attacks this year have been against British security targets but have caused no major casualties.
British Prime Minister John Major, who must call an election by May 22, condemned the latest violence.
"We condemn the taking of life by terrorists which on the face of it this appears to," a spokesman for his office told Reuters.
Last week the IRA issued a statement denying press speculation that they were engaged in a "phoney war" and said they remained committed to ending British rule.
But the guerrillas also said they wanted their political wing, Sinn Fein, to take part in Belfast peace talks from which they are excluded because of IRA violence.
British officials this week dismissed an appeal by Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams for talks, saying such contacts could only take place when there was peace in Northern Ireland.
